D1.evidence: traces/model-on-impl-P10-tlc-counterexample.txt States 1-5; model/Lease-grantor-excerpt.tla lines 8-20 (Elect), 27-36 (StepDown), and 41-48 (Grant); model/README.md lines 125-128 (Interpretation 5); impl/schedule-P10.yaml lines 11-15; traces/impl-own-P10-seed1.jsonl lines 1-2; impl/README.md lines 234-263.
D1.reasoning: In State 2 of the TLC counterexample, n3 is elected leader in term 1 by non-maximal majority Q={n1,n3}, setting promised=[n1|->1, n2|->0, n3|->1] (Elect line 16). In State 3, follower n1 crashes at start; in State 4, c1 requests. In State 4, Grant(n3,c1) (line 46) is disabled because it requires a majority Q of up, connected nodes that already have promised[q]=term[n3]=1, but up follower n2 still has promised[n2]=0 and the model has no action for a leader to advance a follower's promise outside Elect. Meanwhile, Elect(n2) (line 10) is disabled because leader n3 is up, connected, and has term[n3]=1 >= promised[n2]=0, and StepDown(n3) (line 29) is disabled because no node has promised > 1. Thus the model stutters forever (State 5) despite a majority {n2,n3}, storage s, and c1 staying up and connected. (Note: traces/impl-own-P10-seed1.jsonl lines 1-2 is the 2-event trace from the implementation's pre-bootstrap-fix run described in impl/README.md lines 234-248, which also lacked a Grant before the startup voter-configuration barrier in lines 250-263 was added.)
D1.what_would_settle_it: Evidence in the full model (Lease.tla) of an enabled protocol action in State 4 that can advance promised[n2] to term[n3] or allow n2 to elect a higher term while n3 is up and connected, or evidence that the post-bootstrap-fix implementation P10 traces also fail to emit Grant(c1).

D2.evidence: inputs/schedule-format.md lines 13-16 and 20-28; model/README.md lines 140-144 (Interpretations 8-9); impl/README.md lines 89-91 (Interpretation 10) and 157-158 (Interpretation 22); impl/schedule-P2.yaml lines 20-22; impl/schedule-P3.yaml lines 20-22; model/schedule-P2.yaml lines 20-22; model/schedule-P3.yaml lines 17-20; traces/model-on-impl-schedules-results.txt lines 2-3.
D2.reasoning: Both impl/schedule-P2.yaml (lines 20-22) and impl/schedule-P3.yaml (lines 20-22) use {event: Grant, client: c2} as both the final step's trigger (at:) and the schedule's termination trigger (end:), with only one request by c2 in the schedule. inputs/schedule-format.md lines 16 and 28 state that 'the step's action becomes enabled once the predicate has held' and 'the run stops when this trigger fires', without specifying whether each sequential trigger and end: requires a fresh event emitted after the previous step or remains satisfied once observed in the trace. Under model Interpretations 8-9, end: only matches events emitted after the final step (heal in P2, resume in P3) is applied, so a second Grant to c2 would be required and end: is unreachable; under implementation Interpretations 10 and 22, trigger predicates remain true once observed and end: is checked after all actions complete, so the single Grant to c2 satisfies both the final step and end:.
D2.what_would_settle_it: An explicit rule in inputs/schedule-format.md specifying whether step and end triggers match only fresh events emitted after the preceding step's action or behave as monotonic trace predicates that remain true once observed.

D3.evidence: inputs/schedule-format.md lines 38-45 (Actions) and 48-50 (Rules); model/README.md lines 145-148 (Interpretation 10); impl/README.md lines 103-104 (Interpretation 14); model/schedule-P3.yaml line 14; model/schedule-P10.yaml line 14; traces/impl-on-model-schedules-results.txt lines 1-4, 8-9, 14-15, and 21-22.
D3.reasoning: inputs/schedule-format.md line 41 illustrates dynamic aliases (grantor, holder, rest) only in the F1.2 partition example while showing literal process IDs in crash/restart/pause/resume (lines 39-40, 43-44), yet line 50 defines grantor and holder in the general Rules section without restricting them to partition actions. Consequently, the model author permitted grantor and holder as targets of crash, restart, pause, and resume (model/README.md Interpretation 10, used in P1, P3, P6, P10, P12), whereas the implementation author restricted dynamic aliases to partition membership and required explicit process IDs elsewhere (impl/README.md Interpretation 14), causing the implementation compiler to reject those five schedules as UNEXPLAINED.
D3.what_would_settle_it: An explicit grammar or rule in inputs/schedule-format.md stating whether the grantor and holder aliases defined in Rules (line 50) are valid process selectors in F1.1 crash/restart and F1.3 pause/resume actions or only in F1.2 partition lists.
